[[Continuous wavelets]] of [[compact support]] alpha can be built,<ref name=joci-compactly-supported-one-cyclic-wavelets-derived-from-beta-distributions>{{Cite journal|title=Compactly Supported One-cyclic Wavelets Derived from Beta Distributions|journal=Journal of Communication and Information Systems|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/255019827|last1=de Oliveira|first1=Hélio Magalhães|volume=20|pages=27–33|last2=Schmidt|first2=Giovanna Angelis|issue=3|year=2005|doi=10.14209/jcis.2005.17 |doi-access=free|arxiv=1502.02166}}</ref> which are related to the [[beta distribution]].  The process is derived from probability distributions using blur derivative.  These new wavelets have just one cycle, so they are termed unicycle wavelets. They can be viewed as a ''soft variety'' of [[Haar wavelet]]s whose shape is fine-tuned by two parameters <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math>.  Closed-form expressions for beta wavelets and scale functions as well as their spectra are derived.  Their importance is due to the [[Central Limit Theorem]] by Gnedenko and Kolmogorov applied for [[Support_(mathematics)#Compact_support|compactly supported]] signals.<ref name=gnedenko-kolmogorov-limit-distributions>{{Cite book|title=Limit Distributions for Sums of Independent Random Variables|last1=Gnedenko|first1=Boris Vladimirovich|author-link=Boris Vladimirovich Gnedenko|publisher=Addison-Wesley|year=1954|location=Reading, Ma|last2=Kolmogorov|first2=Andrey|author-link2=Andrey Kolmogorov}}</ref>

== Beta distribution ==

The [[beta distribution]] is a continuous [[probability distribution]] defined over the interval <math>0\leq t\leq 1</math>.  It is characterised by a couple of parameters, namely <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math>  according to:

<math>P(t)=\frac{1}{B(\alpha ,\beta )}t^{\alpha -1}\cdot (1-t)^{\beta -1},\quad 1\leq \alpha ,\beta \leq +\infty </math>.

The normalising factor is <math>B(\alpha ,\beta )=\frac{\Gamma (\alpha )\cdot \Gamma (\beta )}{\Gamma (\alpha +\beta )}</math>,

where <math> \Gamma (\cdot )</math> is the [[Gamma function|generalised factorial function of Euler]] and <math>B(\cdot ,\cdot )</math> is the [[Beta function]].<ref name=abramowitz-stegun-davis>{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Mathematical Functions|editor-last=Abramowitz|editor-first=Milton|publisher=[[Dover Publications|Dover]]|year=1968|isbn=0-486-61272-4|location=[[New York City|New York]]|pages=253–294|editor-last2=Stegun|editor-first2=Irene|last=Davis|first=Philip J.|chapter=Gamma Function and Related Functions|chapter-url=http://people.math.sfu.ca/~cbm/aands/page_253.htm|editor-link1=Milton Abramowitz|editor-link2=Irene Stegun|author-link=Philip J. Davis}}</ref>

== Gnedenko-Kolmogorov central limit theorem revisited ==

Let <math>p_{i}(t)</math> be a probability density of the random variable <math>t_{i}</math>, <math>i=1,2,3..N</math> i.e.

<math>p_{i}(t)\ge 0</math>, <math>(\forall t)</math> and <math>\int_{-\infty }^{+\infty }p_{i}(t)dt=1</math>.

Suppose that all variables are independent.

The mean and the variance of a given random variable <math>t_{i}</math> are, respectively

<math>m_{i}=\int_{-\infty }^{+\infty }\tau \cdot p_{i}(\tau )d\tau ,</math> <math>\sigma _{i}^{2}=\int_{-\infty }^{+\infty }(\tau -m_{i})^{2}\cdot p_{i}(\tau )d\tau </math>.

The mean and variance of <math>t</math> are therefore <math>m=\sum_{i=1}^{N}m_{i}</math> and <math>\sigma^2 =\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sigma _{i}^{2}</math>.

The density <math>p(t)</math> of the [[random variable]] corresponding to the sum <math>t=\sum_{i=1}^{N}t_{i}</math> is given by the

'''Central Limit Theorem for distributions of compact support (Gnedenko and Kolmogorov).'''<ref name=gnedenko-kolmogorov-limit-distributions/>

Let <math>\{p_{i}(t)\}</math> be distributions such that <math>Supp\{(p_{i}(t))\}=(a_{i},b_{i})(\forall i)</math>.

Let <math>a=\sum_{i=1}^{N}a_{i}<+\infty </math>, and <math>b=\sum_{i=1}^{N}b_{i}<+\infty</math>.

[[Without loss of generality]] assume that <math>a=0</math> and <math>b=1</math>.
 
The random variable <math>t</math> holds, as <math>N\rightarrow \infty </math>,
<math>p(t)\approx </math> <math>\begin{cases} {k \cdot t^{\alpha }(1-t)^{\beta}}, \\otherwise \end{cases}</math>

where <math>\alpha =\frac{m(m-m^{2}-\sigma ^{2})}{\sigma ^{2}},</math> and <math>\beta =\frac{(1-m)(\alpha +1)}{m}.</math>

== Beta wavelets ==
[[Image:Beta scale and wavelet.jpg|thumb|right|250px|'''Figure. Unicyclic beta scale function and wavelet for different parameters: a) <math>\alpha =4</math>, <math>\beta =3</math> b) <math>\alpha =3</math>, <math>\beta =7</math> c) <math>\alpha =5</math>, <math>\beta =17</math>.''']]

Since <math>P(\cdot |\alpha ,\beta )</math> is [[Unimodality|unimodal]], the wavelet generated by

<math>\psi _{beta}(t|\alpha ,\beta )=(-1)\frac{dP(t|\alpha ,\beta )}{dt}</math> 
has only one-cycle (a negative half-cycle and a positive half-cycle).

The main features of beta wavelets of parameters <math>\alpha</math>  and <math>\beta</math> are:

<math>Supp(\psi )=[ -\sqrt{\frac{\alpha}{\beta}}\sqrt{\alpha + \beta +1},\sqrt{ \frac{\beta }{\alpha }} \sqrt{\alpha +\beta +1}]=[a,b].</math>

<math>lengthSupp(\psi )=T(\alpha ,\beta )=(\alpha +\beta )\sqrt{\frac{\alpha +\beta +1}{\alpha \beta }}.</math>

The parameter <math>R=b/|a| =\beta / \alpha</math> is referred to as “cyclic balance”, and is defined as the ratio between the lengths of the causal and non-causal piece of the wavelet. The instant of transition <math>t_{zerocross}</math> from the first to the second half cycle is given by

<math>t_{zerocross}=\frac{(\alpha -\beta )}{(\alpha +\beta -2)}\sqrt{\frac{\alpha +\beta +1}{\alpha \beta }}.</math>

The (unimodal) scale function associated with the wavelets is given by

<math>\phi _{beta}(t|\alpha ,\beta )=\frac{1}{B(\alpha ,\beta )T^{\alpha +\beta -1}}\cdot (t-a)^{\alpha -1}\cdot (b-t)^{\beta -1},</math> <math>a\leq t\leq b </math>.

A [[closed-form expression]] for first-order beta wavelets can easily be derived. Within their support,

<math>\psi_{beta}(t|\alpha ,\beta ) =\frac{-1}{B(\alpha ,\beta )T^{\alpha +\beta -1}} \cdot [\frac{\alpha -1}{t-a}-\frac{\beta -1}{b-t}] \cdot(t-a)^{\alpha -1} \cdot(b-t)^{\beta -1}</math>

== Beta wavelet spectrum ==

The beta wavelet spectrum can be derived in terms of the Kummer hypergeometric function.<ref name=abramowitz-stegun-slater>{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Mathematical Functions|last=Slater|first=Lucy Joan|publisher=[[Dover Publications|Dover]]|year=1968|isbn=0-486-61272-4|location=[[New York City|New York]]|pages=503–536|chapter-url=http://people.math.sfu.ca/~cbm/aands/page_503.htm|editor-last=Abramowitz|editor-first=Milton|editor-last2=Stegun|editor-first2=Irene|chapter=Confluent Hypergeometric Function|editor-link1=Milton Abramowitz|editor-link2=Irene Stegun|author-link=Lucy Joan Slater}}</ref>

Let <math>\psi _{beta}(t|\alpha ,\beta )\leftrightarrow \Psi _{BETA}(\omega |\alpha ,\beta )</math> denote the [[Fourier transform]] pair associated with the wavelet.

This spectrum is also denoted by <math>\Psi _{BETA}(\omega)</math> for short. It can be proved by applying properties of the Fourier transform that

<math>\Psi _{BETA}(\omega ) =-j\omega \cdot M(\alpha ,\alpha +\beta ,-j\omega (\alpha +\beta )\sqrt{\frac{\alpha +\beta +1}{\alpha \beta}})\cdot exp\{(j\omega \sqrt{\frac{\alpha (\alpha +\beta +1)}{\beta }})\}</math>

where <math>M(\alpha ,\alpha +\beta ,j\nu )=\frac{\Gamma (\alpha +\beta )}{\Gamma (\alpha )\cdot \Gamma (\beta )}\cdot \int_{0}^{1}e^{j\nu t}t^{\alpha -1}(1-t)^{\beta -1}dt</math>.

Only symmetrical <math>(\alpha =\beta )</math> cases have zeroes in the spectrum. A few asymmetric <math>(\alpha \neq \beta )</math> beta wavelets are shown in Fig. Inquisitively, they are parameter-symmetrical in the sense that they hold <math>|\Psi _{BETA}(\omega |\alpha ,\beta )|=|\Psi _{BETA}(\omega |\beta ,\alpha )|.</math>

Higher derivatives may also generate further beta wavelets.  Higher order beta wavelets are defined by
<math>\psi _{beta}(t|\alpha ,\beta )=(-1)^{N}\frac{d^{N}P(t|\alpha ,\beta )}{dt^{N}}.</math>

This is henceforth referred to as an <math>N</math>-order beta wavelet. They exist for order <math>N\leq Min(\alpha ,\beta )-1</math>. After some algebraic handling, their closed-form expression can be found:

<math>\Psi _{beta}(t|\alpha ,\beta ) =\frac{(-1)^{N}}{B(\alpha ,\beta ) \cdot T^{\alpha +\beta -1}} \sum_{n=0}^{N}sgn(2n-N)\cdot \frac{\Gamma (\alpha )}{\Gamma (\alpha -(N-n))}(t-a)^{\alpha -1-(N-n)} \cdot \frac{\Gamma (\beta )}{\Gamma (\beta -n)}(b-t)^{\beta -1-n}.</math>

An <math>N^{th}</math>-order beta wavelet has <math>N</math> [[Vanishing moment|vanishing moments]], and is therefore insensitive to polynomial trends of degree up to <math>N-1</math>. <ref name="Oliveira2005">{{cite journal

== Application ==
Wavelet theory is applicable to several subjects. All wavelet transforms may be considered forms of time-frequency representation for continuous-time (analog) signals and so are related to [[harmonic analysis]]. Almost all practically useful discrete wavelet transforms use discrete-time filter banks. Similarly, Beta wavelet<ref name=joci-compactly-supported-one-cyclic-wavelets-derived-from-beta-distributions/><ref name=beta-wavelets-synthesis-application>{{Cite journal|title=Beta wavelets. Synthesis and application to lossy image compression|journal=Advances in Engineering Software|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220291306|last1=Ben Amar|first1=Chokri|volume=36|pages=459–474|last2=Zaied|first2=Mourad|publisher=Elsevier|issue=7|year=2005|last3=Alimi|first3=Adel M.|doi= 10.1016/j.advengsoft.2005.01.013}}</ref> and its derivative are utilized in several real-time engineering applications such as image compression,<ref name=beta-wavelets-synthesis-application/> bio-medical signal compression,<ref name=jmma-electrocardiogram-signal-compression>{{Cite journal|title=Electrocardiogram Signal compression Using Beta Wavelets|journal=Journal of Mathematical Modelling and Algorithms|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257581974|last1=Kumar|first1=Ranjeet|volume=11|last2=Kumar|first2=Anil|publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer Verlag]]|issue=3|doi=10.1007/s10852-012-9181-9|year=2012|last3=Pandey|first3=Rajesh K.|pages=235–248|s2cid=4667379}}</ref><ref name=cee-beta-wavelet-based-ecg-signal-compression>{{Cite journal|title=Beta wavelet based ECG signal compression using lossless encoding with modified thresholding|journal=Computers & Electrical Engineering|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/256918193|last1=Kumar|first1=Ranjeet|volume=39|pages=130–140|last2=Kumar|first2=Anil|publisher=[[Elsevier]]|issue=1|doi=10.1016/j.compeleceng.2012.04.008|year=2013|last3=Pandey|first3=Rajesh K.}}</ref> image recognition [9]<ref name=ix-conf-paper>{{Cite book|chapter=Training of the Beta wavelet networks by the frames theory: Application to face recognition|title=2008 First Workshops on Image Processing Theory, Tools and Applications|last1=Zaied|first1=Mourad|last2=Jemai|first2=Olfa|publisher=[[IEEE]]|doi=10.1109/IPTA.2008.4743756|year=2008|issn=2154-5111|eissn=2154-512X|last3=Ben Amar|first3=Chokri|pages=1–6|isbn=978-1-4244-3321-6|s2cid=12230926}}</ref> etc.
